Understand the possessor-plus-subject structure behind present have.
teachingPoints.prompt: How does MSA commonly express present possession instead of using a normal verb meaning have?
teachingPoints.answer: With a word meaning with, at, or to — عِنْدَ, لَدَى, or لِـ — plus the possessor (often an attached pronoun), then the possessed thing as the subject.

teachingPoints.objective: Attach the first-person plural possessor to the common possession expression.
teachingPoints.prompt: Complete “we have time”: ___ وَقْتٌ (___ waqtun).

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish a nominative possessed subject from a preposition's genitive complement.
teachingPoints.prompt: In عِنْدَهُ سَيَّارَةٌ, why is the car noun not genitive after the possession expression?
teachingPoints.answer: Because it is the nominative subject; عِنْدَ governs only its attached pronoun, not the possessed noun.

teachingPoints.objective: Interpret definiteness of the possessed thing as a known item.
teachingPoints.prompt: How does عِنْدِي الْمِفْتَاحُ differ from saying that I have an unspecified key?
teachingPoints.answer: It means I have the key, a known definite item.

teachingPoints.objective: Produce the formal first-person possession form before a question noun.
teachingPoints.prompt: I have a question, using لَدَى: ___ سُؤَالٌ.

teachingPoints.objective: Express feminine possession with the belonging construction.
teachingPoints.prompt: Complete “she has a house” (belonging), using لِـ: ___ بَيْتٌ (___ baytun).

teachingPoints.objective: Pick the everyday neutral MSA word for having something.
teachingPoints.prompt: Which MSA possession expression is the common, neutral everyday choice for “have”?

teachingPoints.objective: Recognize the exception particle and its restrictive use with negation.
Interpret a negative exception as a positive restriction in English.
teachingPoints.prompt: Why does مَا جَاءَ إِلَّا طَالِبٌ translate naturally with only rather than just except?
teachingPoints.answer: Negation excludes everyone else: no one came except a student, so only a student came.

teachingPoints.objective: Retain subject nominative in a negative restrictive sentence without a stated larger group.
teachingPoints.prompt: Complete “only Zayd came”: مَا جَاءَ إِلَّا ___ (mā jāʾa illā ___).

teachingPoints.objective: Keep object accusative in an only-one-book construction.
teachingPoints.prompt: I read only one book: لَمْ أَقْرَأْ إِلَّا ___.

teachingPoints.objective: Use accusative for an excluded member of an expressed group in an affirmative sentence.
teachingPoints.prompt: Complete “the teachers came except one teacher”: جَاءَ الْمُعَلِّمُونَ إِلَّا ___ (jāʾa al-muʿallimūna illā ___).

teachingPoints.objective: Mark the excluded noun correctly in an affirmative exception with a named group.
teachingPoints.prompt: In MSA, what case follows إِلَّا (illā) in an affirmative sentence that names the larger group, such as “the students came except …”?

teachingPoints.objective: Let the sentence role set the case after illā when no group is named.
teachingPoints.prompt: When a negative sentence names no larger group before إِلَّا (illā), what decides the case of the word after it?
teachingPoints.answer: Its role in the sentence, as if illā were absent: a subject is nominative, an object accusative.

teachingPoints.objective: Read negation plus illā as restriction to one thing.
teachingPoints.prompt: What English meaning does negation plus إِلَّا (illā) usually produce?
teachingPoints.answer: Only: “not … except X” means only X.

teachingPoints.objective: Identify specification as clarification of amount or respect.
teachingPoints.prompt: What question does tamyīz answer after an amount or comparison?
teachingPoints.answer: Of what? or In what respect?

teachingPoints.objective: Retain the genuine substance noun in the measure example.

teachingPoints.objective: Use singular accusative after twenty despite English plural translation.

teachingPoints.prompt: What does هَوَاءً clarify in طَابَ الْمَكَانُ هَوَاءً?
teachingPoints.answer: The respect in which the place is pleasant: its air.

teachingPoints.objective: Give a specifying tamyīz noun its usual formal shape.
teachingPoints.prompt: In formal MSA, what definiteness and case does a tamyīz noun usually have?

teachingPoints.objective: Keep the specified noun singular after tens.
teachingPoints.prompt: After a number such as thirty, is the tamyīz noun singular or plural in Arabic?
teachingPoints.answer: Singular, even when English uses a plural.

teachingPoints.objective: Separate one/two agreement from the opposite-gender zone.
teachingPoints.prompt: How do numbers one and two differ from the 3–10 polarity pattern?
teachingPoints.answer: They commonly follow the noun and agree in gender instead of showing opposite gender.

teachingPoints.prompt: Complete “thirty cities”: ثَلَاثُونَ ___ (thalāthūna ___).

teachingPoints.objective: Apply reverse gender agreement to numerals three through ten.
teachingPoints.prompt: For numbers 3–10, how does the numeral’s gender relate to the gender of the counted noun’s singular?
teachingPoints.answer: It is the opposite (polarity): a masculine noun takes a numeral with ة, a feminine noun takes one without.

teachingPoints.objective: Recall the connector for a later sequential step.

teachingPoints.answer: Fa- marks immediate sequence or result; thumma marks a later step after some interval.

teachingPoints.objective: Keep Moroccan recognition aids qualified rather than universalizing them across the Maghreb.
teachingPoints.prompt: Do all Maghrebi varieties, such as Algerian and Tunisian Arabic, mark the present with the Moroccan prefix ka-?
teachingPoints.answer: No. Many Algerian and Tunisian speakers use the bare imperfect, such as nekteb (I write); grammar, vocabulary and spelling vary across the region.

teachingPoints.prompt: In Moroccan Darija kan-fham (I understand), what does the n- after ka- mark?
teachingPoints.answer: First-person singular (I); ka- alone is the present marker.

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish gemination in II from vowel lengthening in III within one root family.
teachingPoints.prompt: What distinguishes the root shapes of Form II and Form III?
teachingPoints.answer: II doubles the middle radical; III lengthens the vowel after the first radical to ā.

teachingPoints.objective: Recognize the fighting verb as a genuine Form III lexical item.

teachingPoints.prompt: Does every Form III verb literally mean doing something mutually with someone?
teachingPoints.answer: No. Learn each verb's meaning in context; association is only a useful tendency.

teachingPoints.objective: Anticipate the causative or intensive sense of a doubled-middle verb.
teachingPoints.prompt: What two kinds of meaning does Form II (faʿʿala) commonly add to a root?
teachingPoints.answer: Causative (making someone do it) or intensive / repeated action.

teachingPoints.objective: Anticipate the interactive sense of a long-ā Form III verb.
teachingPoints.prompt: What relationship does Form III (fāʿala) often add to an action?
teachingPoints.answer: Acting with, toward, or in relation to another person (association or interaction).

teachingPoints.objective: Recognize the lexical waking-someone verb as Form IV.
Recognize the sending verb without demanding an English cause paraphrase.
Retain submission and becoming-Muslim meanings of the individual verb.
Apply the sound Form IV present vowels rather than copying the past prefix.
teachingPoints.prompt: أَخْرَجَ → he brings out: ___.

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish active and passive participle vowels in the sound pattern.
teachingPoints.prompt: In sound Form IV participles, how does the vowel before the final radical distinguish active from passive?
teachingPoints.answer: Active has i; passive has a.

teachingPoints.objective: Avoid treating a productive causative family as one fixed lexical translation.
teachingPoints.prompt: Must a Form IV verb always be translated literally as cause to?
teachingPoints.answer: No. The pattern is a family clue; learn the individual lexical meaning.

teachingPoints.objective: Produce the sound bringing-out maṣdar with initial kasrah and long ā.
teachingPoints.prompt: أَخْرَجَ → its maṣdar, bringing out: ___.

teachingPoints.objective: Expect a Form IV verb to make someone do the base action.
teachingPoints.prompt: What meaning does Form IV (afʿala) most commonly add to a Form I verb?
teachingPoints.answer: Causative: making someone or something do the Form I action.

teachingPoints.objective: Keep the Form IV initial hamza pronounced after a prefix.
teachingPoints.prompt: Is the initial hamza of a Form IV past verb a joining hamza (waṣl) or a cutting hamza (qaṭʿ)?
teachingPoints.answer: A cutting hamza (hamzat qaṭʿ): it is always pronounced.

teachingPoints.objective: Link the two ta- forms to their doubled versus long-vowel source patterns.
teachingPoints.prompt: Which earlier forms underlie V and VI, and what shape does each retain?
teachingPoints.answer: V relates to II and retains the doubled middle radical; VI relates to III and retains long ā after the first radical.

teachingPoints.objective: Recall acquiring knowledge as the inward counterpart of teaching.
Recognize training oneself/practicing as a Form V lexical item.
Retain the reciprocal meeting verb's singular dictionary form.
Recall the cooperation verb as shared action.

teachingPoints.prompt: He learned, Form V counterpart of عَلَّمَ: ___.

teachingPoints.objective: Recall consultation with others without confusing reciprocal sense with plural inflection.
Recognize the exchange verb in its singular dictionary form.
Recognize reaching mutual understanding as an individual lexical meaning.
Separate MSA verb-first agreement from the semantic plurality of reciprocal events.
teachingPoints.prompt: In MSA, what number does a Form VI verb such as تَقَابَلَ take when it comes before an explicit plural subject?
teachingPoints.answer: Singular: verb-first agreement applies even though the meaning is reciprocal.

teachingPoints.objective: Add actual plural agreement for an independent they-form.
teachingPoints.prompt: They met each other, from تَقَابَلَ (standalone plural): ___.

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Form V: inward or acquired action
teachingPoints.objective: Relate a ta- Form V verb to its Form II counterpart as self-directed.
teachingPoints.prompt: What does Form V (tafaʿʿala) often do to the meaning of its Form II counterpart?
teachingPoints.answer: It makes it reflexive or middle: the action turns back toward the subject.

teachingPoints.objective: Expect mutual or shared action from a tafāʿala verb.
teachingPoints.prompt: What kind of action does Form VI (tafāʿala) typically express?
teachingPoints.answer: Reciprocal or shared action between two sides or within a group.

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish a prefixed n from an inserted and possibly assimilated t.
teachingPoints.prompt: How do the structural clues of Forms VII and VIII differ?
teachingPoints.answer: VII begins in-; VIII inserts t after the first root consonant, sometimes with assimilation.

teachingPoints.prompt: What kind of meaning does Form VII (infaʿala) typically have?
teachingPoints.answer: Passive-reflexive: the subject undergoes a change, with no outside agent named.
